newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina seeks FBI's help in photographer's murder. [CORRECTED 22:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Argentina seeks FBI's help in photographer's murder. [CORRECTED 22:25 GMT]

text.p: Argentine authorities have sought the help of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation to hunt the killers of a news photographer found shot and burned in a car last weekend, officials said on Thursday.
Buenos Aires Province's Gov. Eduardo Duhalde, called the murder of Jose Luis Cabezas the worst such atrocity since the reign of the death squads in the 1970s.

"Given the complexity of the investigation that needs a great deal of expertise, it's very likely the FBI may help us. I have spoken with officials from the organisation today and may receive a visit from them (Friday)," Duhalde said.

Duhalde, the main contender to succeed President Carlos Menem for the Peronist candidacy in 1999's elections, has a summer residence close to where Cabezas' charred body was found on a dirt track outside the beach resort of Pinamar, southeast of Buenos Aires, early on Saturday.

Cabezas had been handcuffed, shot in the head, doused with fuel and set on fire, probably while he was still alive. His body was so badly burned it had to be identified by his car keys, watch and dental records.
It was a gruesome reminder of "Dirty War" tactics used from the early 1970s until the return of democracy in 1983.

"There has been no case of these characteristics since the democracy returned. We must hunt and capture those responsible because we've no guarantee they won't do this again," the governor said. "But we must not be afraid. The killers of Cabezas are a wretched group with the whole of society against them."
Duhalde has offered a $300,000 reward and a pardon for anyone coming forward with information about the killers.

Thousands of people marched in silence through Buenos Aires on Wednesday in solidarity with Cabezas' colleagues at Noticias, Argentina's top-selling news weekly magazine. It has been critical of Menem's government and recently revealed cases of corruption inside the Buenos Aires Province police.
Duhalde said speculation that police from his own force, or officers fired as a result of the Noticias stories, could be involved in the killing "stops me from sleeping."
"You cannot have foxes investigating a massacre in a hen-house," Radical Party leader Rodolfo Terragno said.

Many Argentines were worried the case will take the same dead end road as investigations into anti-Jewish bomb attacks here in 1992 and 1994 (corrects from 1982 and 1984), in which more than 100 people died.
At a press meeting with Menem, a colleague of Cabezas handed the president a picture of the dead photographer. "Sir, this is so that you don't forget our colleague," she told him.
